title: The Kid & I
full_review:
Tom Arnold writes and stars in "The Kid & I" (Wheels Up), a well-intentioned but clumsy buddy comedy -- loosely based on Arnold's real-life experiences with his neighbor's disabled son -- centering on washed-up actor Bill Williams (a self-effacing Arnold), who (like Arnold) once enjoyed fleeting fame when he appeared in "True Lies" with Arnold Schwarzenegger. Since then, his personal and professional lives have run a neck-and-neck race down the drain.

The movie opens with Bill preparing to commit suicide with sleeping pills and booze.

But when the overdose fails to achieve its intended results, Bill awakes to news that his agent (Henry Winkler) has landed him a job writing and co-starring in a cheesy action film with a physically challenged teenager, Aaron (Eric Gores, Arnold's real next-door neighbor), whose wealthy businessman father (Joe Mantegna) is footing the bill for the project.

Bill sees it as a chance for a comeback until he learns that their financier only intends to show the film at a private screening for his son's 18th birthday to fulfill the boy's dream of being a movie star.

Unfunny comic complications ensue that mostly involve witless exchanges between Arnold and Richard Edson, who plays a derelict Bill hires as his personal assistant.

Despite a slapdash look, in addition to its name cast, the film boasts cameos by heavyweights such as Shaquille O'Neal, Schwarzenegger and Jamie Lee Curtis.

Exuding disarming optimism, newcomer Gores, who has cerebral palsy, offers a refreshingly positive image of disabled persons. As Aaron, Gores bubbles with a boyish blend of mischief and insecurities, especially when it comes to girls. He makes sure that Bill writes in some romance with his object of infatuation, real-life model Arielle Kebbel, with whom he gets to share an achingly awkward kiss.

Director Penelope Spheeris is on the record as saying that she wanted to make an uplifting film, stating, "There is enough negativity in the world ... we should not manufacture more." Admirable sentiments, but apart from a few sweet moments, the film's heartfelt and ultimately life-affirming message is saddled by inept writing and direction.

In one scene Linda Hamilton -- playing Bill's ex-wife, Susan, a big-time Hollywood producer who lends her weight to the cause -- confides that "I would never make a movie like this if I knew it was for public consumption."

Unfortunately for audiences, this one is.

The film contains some crude language and humor, and brief drug references. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
